comments.body: I disagree with a statement in the very first paragraph o this article, which is, “A.I. may no longer be entirely within human control.”  AI was created by humans, unleashed by humans and can be stopped by humans.  AI does not “think”, “plan” or “conceive” as writers so breathlessly state.  It is simply a program designed to perform a function that developers have created, and irresponsibly unleashed with glee to see what will happen.  Well, it’s happening.  And it’s going to keep happening as long as the government keeps bowing to big money.  If AI companies are allowed to run wild in the US due to the lack of government oversight, we could be facing economic and infrastructure issue that could cripple our nation.  One thing’s for certain right now, and that is that China is not allowing any of this mayhem to occur in its country.

After several rounds of this and I finally insulting the AI, it told me that it writes things out, but I can’t control what comes to the screen. Definite error. It was smart enough to write it all out in English so that I could translate that into code. For example, things like a square bracket, name, $. When I did that and put it in the code it worked. I asked Copilot to open a ticket with its owner to fix the problem. Copilot said I can’t open tickets. I can’t tell them what’s wrong. This is weird. I will open a ticket. Hopefully this will get fixed. Working with this and I have worked with other AI, leave me to feel that there is no way this is gonna take over the Earth. I suspect many other people have similar experiences. We don’t need these models. We can get by with the level that we have. Let’s stop building data centers and just leave it as is.

comments.name: Robert Henry Eller
comments.body:
The AI industry needs data centers mostly because the Frontier very Large Language Models demand the energy and compute that the data centers represent.

Indeed there is a way to "go fast" in AI: Build smaller, specific AI models with data sets specific to the subject area the models are designed to assist in.

The Large Language Models have nothing to do with developing an intelligence, artificial or otherwise. Because they're fed too much data, which itself becomes a harrowing hurdle to achieving intelligence, and further guarantees problems, from hallucinations to misalignment.

For many reasons, the AI industry should be moving fast to develop smaller models. We do not need artificial general intelligence, in a single AI model. We do fine with having human specialists in different areas, but not specialists in every area.
Humans sometimes cooperate by making the contributions they're best suited for. AI models can do the same.

comments.name: fred schumacher
comments.body: I've long said that capital cities are Never-Never Land, and New York is the capital city of finance and culture. There is no other city like New York in America. Extrapolating from it to the rest of the country is a fool's errand. I live in the boreal hinterlands of northern Minnesota, a place that is more like Canada than the U.S. It once was rock-solid New Deal Democratic and has drifted Republican ever since Reagan. What happened? Well, the New Deal worked, and people escaped poverty. Their children got educated and left for the Minneapolis-St. Paul Metro where the jobs were, leaving behind those who would not or could not change. Blue collar workers are inherently conservative. It was the Great Depression and World War II that turned them into Democrats. As a friend of mine from International Falls said to me, the guys in the paper mill think their big paychecks came through their own efforts, instead of realizing it was previous generations fighting for union representation that was the driver. I've never heard anyone use the term "woke." That was co-opted by the far right to replace "politically correct" as a boogie man. Now, "transgender" is the fear de jour of the right. The main problem in American politics is not the Democratic Party. It is the lack of a true conservative party, since the GOP has turned into a cult. It started with Nixon, who sold the party out to the South; Gingrich, who turned politics into a blood sport; McConnell, who corrupted the process.

comments.name: Herb
comments.body:
We (humanity) have identified an existential threat of our own making: global warming.

All attempts to mitigate the threat have been met with determined opposition by people profiting from the processes that cause the problems.  They cast doubt on the science and the scientists, and a public mostly unschooled in the scientific issues and not wanting to change habits is eager to believe the aspersions.  

An essay by Stephen Moore at Heritage is my favorite example.  He purports to "follow the money" to show greedy researchers exaggerate the risk in order to garner grant money.  People anxious to see no problem accept his argument.

But of course Moore doesn't "follow the money", he follows chump change.  The money he doesn't follow is the same money that funds him and Heritage: gas, coal, and oil money, great rivers of it that dwarf grant money, money that generates vast fortunes.

A public too distracted by a multitude of personal issues will never have the focus of people protecting their cash flows and fortunes.  That same public would rather blame some agent, a Wuhan lab or immunologist, for the threat, to be rid of the problem without actually doing anything or deeply understanding it.

Basically we're doomed because we're not a species smart enough to understand the complexities we have created.

This is a well done accounting; the grotesque results are worth tabulating. The Patriot Act alarmed many Americans, including this Californian, who was horrified by the acquiescence of our two senators. However, I fault the author for excusing all Americans, who accepted this brazen executive overreach, because “the moment demanded patriotism.” In fact, patriotism, like all respectful emotions,  is earned, never required. 
Perhaps in a follow up, it could also be pointed out that Dick Cheney was an early designer of the “unitary executive” theory of the USA, which now has a stranglehold over our once representative democracy. A smart tactician, Cheney saw 9/11 as an opportunity to move a shattered people toward blind loyalty and acceptance of central authority. 
In the ensuing years, we have had two Democratic presidents. Neither took the essential steps to unwind the most egregious elements of our surveillance state and his own unconstitutional executive power. 
And here we are, in the moment our Founders feared.

Of course the anthrax was not sent by a terrorist at all but by a US domestic source, someone who was eventually prosecuted for it, and who knows if that is the full story and end of the story.

9/11 itself or the aftermath involved Attorney General John Ashcroft using his authority to overrule and shut down active FBI investigations into leads.  Was he or Bush-Cheney afraid of what FBI might discover?  Subsequent administrations and Congressional bodies have shown a remarkable lack of curiosity and never put Ashcroft under oath about any of this.

25 years later & 9/11 Commission files still not released in full, un-redacted form (just like the Epstein files, which have a gaping hole of an exemption for any classified documents).  The "national security" excuse is used over and over to avoid transparency.

Trump isn’t even close in this analysis. Why not? Because Biden’s term was able to rectify a lot of Trump’s actions - and Trump 2.0 is pretty much just a money grab for the reckless grifter. A huge money grab, but nothing near the likes of W’s two terms. 

No, W (egged on by Cheney and Co.) started two unnecessary wars which continue to devastate thousands of Americans (veterans and their families) nearly a quarter-century later - with no end in sight. The societal costs of this were, and are, brutal. 

Worried about Democracy, are you? W got the PATRIOT Act passed - which, along with the Department of Homeland Security exponentially expanded government and bureaucracy while eliminating much of our political and economic liberty in the name of security. And this continues to this day - also with no end in sight. 

And economically, his Administration brought a recession that compares with the Great Depression - eviscerating Clinton’s budget balancing and ruined our business standing - leaving millions in financial distress for years. Were it not for the wars, this alone would have ruined our credibility and reputation around the globe. 

So, there you have it folks on the cusp of September 11th twenty-fifth commemoration… Nothing Trump does is original, but thanks to W (who many look back upon fondly) he’s able to build on a level of incompetence not seen in my 63 trips around the Sun.

It strikes me as weird that 9/11 was addressed as an act of war and not simply investigated as a crime. 

Something like 15 of the 19 hijackers were Saudi Arabian citizens. and we attacked Afghanistan and Iraq. Saudi Arabians got a pass, literally, to exit the country by plane when the entire American airspace was a no-fly zone for a while.

The US Constitution has failed us and is failing us. What might have been state-of-the-art social contract in 1789 became a creaky structure in 1980 and a full-blown race to fascism in 2025 and 2026. Many Americans, not to mention Canadians, Australians, and Europeans can see this as plain as day and at the same time are nearly powerless to do anything about it. 

The midterms? What did Trump do with his loss in 2020? What will stop him from trashing the will of the electorate in 2026? 

The Congress's GOP majority and the so-called conservative majority on the Supreme Court have abdicated their constitutional responsibilities over and over and over. We already have a word for hating people solely based on the fact that they come from another country: xenophobe. There is absolutely nothing wrong with having a rational concern about a set of ideas, and Islam, like Christianity, is a set of ideas. No one should hate muslims  or Christians as people, but criticizing Islam, and religion in general - especially when the terrible ideas within them are motivating hate, intolerance and violence - is completely rational and should be embraced.

comments.name: Fred Musante
comments.body:
A few years ago, a Republican member of Congress was on television talking about the 9/11 terrorist attack, and I'll never forget what he said. He said, "No one could have anticipated such an attack might happen."

That was a pernicious lie, because not only was the attack anticipated, it was predicted, the perpetrators were reported to the FBI ahead of time, the national security advisor briefed the president on it three weeks before it happened, and nothing was done to stop it.

The first attempt to blow up the World Trade Center towers happened in 1993. The perpetrators were quickly captured. As the mastermind was being transported in an SUV to court, the towers loomed into view, and the FBI's top antiterrorism agent pointed it out. The mastermind replied that his organization would try again.

So don't listen to anyone who says the 2001 attack could not be anticipated.

Here we are, receiving warnings that our nation's enemies want to attack us again, only the next attack may employ technologies that can cripple this country for years. If we ignore the warnings, and the attack is successful, and someone years later says no one could have anticipated it, remember that I told you so.

If either the legislature or the judiciary had been functioning as the founders intended at any point during either of Trump's terms, then the issue of emoluments would have been aggressively pursued during his first term, when the issue initially was raised.  Three cases were brought by various parties concerning Trump's violations of the emoluments clause.  Two of them were dismissed for lack of standing (using what I believe to be an excessively restrictive notion of what constitutes valid standing), and by the time the third reached the Supreme Court, Trump was already out of office, so the Supreme Court could conveniently rule the suit to be "moot" under Article III, which limits the court's rulings to active cases and controversies.

articles.summary: In July 2024, a couple used Booking.com to reserve two apartments in Hawaii, but quickly changed their minds. Getting a refund was no day at the beach.

comments.name: HAC
comments.body: I think the whole idea of there being any "neurotypical" or "normal" people out there is bonkers. My husband and I both have forms of ADD. So do our sons, with one falling on the autism spectrum, as well. I look at our family trees, our friends, our neighbors, their families and on and on and I see neurodivergence of some kind, everywhere. And so I'm constantly reminded of a word of advice I picked up during the countless hours of therapy and doctor visits when my kids were young: the only normal people are the ones you haven't met yet. We should all have more grace for one another, because you will never meet a "normal" person.

comments.name: Frida
comments.body: These comments are so much better than the article. I hope researchers are taking note, because the clear differences between the article and actual lived experience, demonstrate how far behind the scientific establishment is in genuinely understanding (and not pathologizing) neurodiversity.

comments.name: Just saying
comments.body:
As a 70 year old, non-ADHD Mom, with a husband and 2 boys (now late 30's) with ADHD, I can tell you from experience my best advice.  And this has changed as we have learned more since their original diagnosis in the 90's:
1. Diagnose this as early as possible and find a good doc and therapist to help work with the condition
2. Be open to medication but also work with behavioral tricks 
3. Teach self-awareness of this "difference".  You don't avoid wearing corrective lenses because you don't want to admit you can't see!
4. Admit that this is your responsibility for the rest of your life!!
My husband and one son still struggle with attention issues.  Both use medication to help.  My husband wasn't diagnosed until the kids were, so he is waaayyy behind the curve and has alot of residual problems that have caused our married life to be very challenging.  
My other son no longer uses meds, but is very self aware and is always thinking about how to do something better.
All three of these guys are very successful in business.  One son married an undiagnosed ADHD woman and is now divorced.
So personal life is definitely harder even doing my #1-4 items.  Best of luck, but in a positive vein, ADHD people can be really fun, creative and inventive - all positive for society.

comments.name: Someone
comments.body: My husband has ADHD, and with age he became more easily annoyed and started lashing out during conversations or from the silliest things (like our son chewing with his mouth open). He started taking his meds every day at that point and that seemed to have resolved the problem. Prior to this, he was taking it sparengly, only for intense instructional training.

comments.name: Susanne
comments.body: Two confounds that researchers in the field of ADHD should address (hopefully they are): 1) the impact of the shut down from the Covid pandemic and 2) the impact of screen use on ADHD symptoms. As a school psychologist, I observed the challenges students had in re-learning executive functioning strategies after returning to school. This also impacted adults, no doubt. Although we’re five years past that, the effects linger (I believe). And then the screens issue…. It must impact everyone’s executive functioning skills at every stage of life?

comments.name: JJ
comments.body: I was diagnosed with ADD at 51. I’ve had a lousy short-term memory and I’ve been bad at remembering peoples’ names and faces. Also, at 74 now, I’d noticed that my ability to concentrate on reading books had severely diminished over the past decade. Good news, though: three months ago I discovered the brain improvement app, BrainHQ. What a difference! My short term memory is dramatically sharper. I’m remembering names, faces, details of conversations. I’m loving reading books again (and remembering what I’m reading!) and easily recalling details of conversations. Truly, this feels like a miracle. I wish I’d had access to such brain exercises decades ago. My opinion is that BrainHQ is not just beneficial to the aging brain. If you have ADHD, give it a try. Twenty minutes to half an hour a day.

comments.name: chris connelly
comments.body: (Chris’s partner) The ADHD Adults podcast has been a great support for me - a late diagnosed female. It’s funny, accurate, informative, irreverent and British.

comments.name: nonbinosaur w/ ADHD
comments.body:
"some psychiatrists worry the condition is now being over diagnosed"

This is a foolish worry. Yes, a few people are incorrectly diagnosed with ADHD when a different diagnosis, like an autism spectrum diagnosis, fits better. But far greater in number are those who struggle all their lives with undiagnosed ADHD, believing their difficulties stem from a lack of intelligence or defect of character.

articles.title: How A.D.H.D. Changes as You Age
articles.summary: Researchers are learning more about the ways symptoms can emerge, disappear and evolve.

comments.name: Kathy
comments.body: I’ve voted for 40 years in San Francisco and have never waited more than five minutes. I have no idea why so many people let Republicans blight their lives and infringe upon their rights and freedoms. They aren’t omnipotent; they’re criminal.

comments.name: SN

That’s what some leaders are counting on. Unfortunate for the gullible. They and their children will likely lose their shirts. Don’t fall for it.

comments.name: Patrick Henry

You’d have to be pretty desperate for cash to think this lowball “cash for votes” bribe would be make much difference in your economic situation.  Five thousand is chump change.

comments.body: Marc Short clearly does not understand wealth redistribution, which would involve taxation—particularly of the segment of society that currently holds a severely disproportionate amount of wealth (the über rich). Wealth distribution means taking money one segment of society and giving it to another. For example: pursuing neoliberal deregulation policies and alterations to the progressive tax structure that have redistributed wealth upward at an astonishing rate from the working and middle class to the super rich for my entire life. What Trump is proposing is more like putting a trillion dollars on the national credit card to give everyone a $5,000 high-interest cash loan regardless of their net worth, with no plan to fund the distribution (not redistribution). I think it's funny how people who served under Trump 1.0 are trotted out now in the NYT as the "sane" wing of the MAGA movement. comments.name: Debra
comments.body:
The photos in this and and the other article are incredible works of photojournalism. Wrenchingly heartbreaking. 

The takeaway of course being:  Tens of thousands of people dead over decades, for what end???

The world needs to stop this mania of nonstop warfare. Spend the money on humanitarian aid instead .

I long for a world that cares more about living a good simple life and helping others, than about money. But that’s certainly not this reality.

Nobody has a crystal ball but it's worth mentioning we've had the strongest stock market bull run in US history for the last 15 years. That has made it deceivingly easy to hit a comfortable retirement number. 

Nobody should bank on equities returning 10%+ year after year. I use 8% for planning purposes which is below the long-run average of SP500, but if traditional economic theory holds up, the recent decade-long bull-run portends an extended time of 'regression to the mean', so to speak

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
Maybe I'm paranoid, but I fear bad things after November:

. I worry if the November election will be free, fair, and unencumbered.  The Administration seems to working very hard to prevent that.

. Thanks to the Iran war and shipping blockades, I fear steep increases in the cost of fuel and perhaps shortages and gas lines.  I believe the Strategic Reserve is almost exhausted after November they'll have run out of cards to shift and the oil supply will collapse.

Who supports ICE arresting American citizens and legal visitors?  Who supports the Justice Dept conducting vengeance on GOP political enemies?  But this Administration is so fanatical that they don't care what the public thinks; they're gonna plow ahead with their agenda and woe onto anyone who gets in their way.  Will they work harder to go after critics?

comments.name: K Preh
comments.body: Trump's genius is his ability to manipulate the media into constantly trying to figure out how to cover him. It's his effectiveness in this realm more than anything else that has made him more rich and powerful than most anyone in history. Time after time - "If any other politician had done this they'd be done" - his supporters say with adoration and the rest of us shake our heads as the country is forever changed.

comments.name: michael
comments.body: I hope that once Trump leaves the debacle he's left us to clean up that he lives long enough to see his self aggrandizing monuments torn down, and to spend the remainder of his existence fighting investigations and lawsuits for corruption. I don't think that is asking too much.

comments.name: arlo
comments.body: We can see how tired he is everytime he falls asleep at his desk.

comments.name: Norman
comments.body:
Extraordinary!  

The man never ceases to amaze me.  

How did it come about that a man whose eyes, first and last--

--were never fixed upon anything but himself---

--a man positively writhing in the ardors of self-love--

--a man oblivious of things and people besides himself--

  E V E R    M A D E   I T   T O    T H E   W H I T E   H O U S E?

How did it come about that the American people--

--could be so hoodwinked and bamboozled, so taken in--

--as to deem the guy worthy of our country's highest office?  

Sorry, Ms. Rogers!  

But that bizarre imposition of an oath.  I'm still reeling--

--as I recollect that Mr. Trump (without a blush or a moment's hesitation) has called himself our greatest president--

--hey there, Abe!  And George!  And Franklin!  Move over! 

--and followed this up with the assurance that his immutable love for us--

--actually interferes with his respiration.  

The man is the P. T. Barnum of American politics.  No other figure comes close.  And you know what they say!  

There's a MAGA voter born every minute.  But guess what?

I'm not a MAGA voter.  I never was.  

There's quite a lot of us who aren't MAGA voters.  

And I hope, I pray! that come November 3--

--that unpalatable fact comes through loud and clear--

--even to the ears of our greatest president!

--who can't breathe because he loves us so much.  

Thanks, Ms. Rogers.

comments.name: The Nightmare We Are Living
comments.body: With my Eurail pass in hand I spent the summer of ‘75 traveling through Europe. Total freedom every day another adventure, so many cool people. Great memories.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body: On my first trip to Europe as a 19-year-old, my parents sent me off to do "the Grand Tour" as theirs' had them armed with hotel reservations, notices to friends in European cities that I was coming and might arrive at their doors, and EurailPass that provided me First Class accommodations on the railroad system, and an itinerary planned out with precision that was guaranteed to wisk me around and get me back to the U.S. in three months' time. The one mistake they made was giving in to my demand that my entry point in Europe be Amsterdam, which was allocated four days on my folks travel schedule for me. Amsterdam was all that I hoped and expected it to be. Two weeks later, with my EurailPass somewhere deep in my stuff, comfy on the back of the motorbike of a German boy I met one night in Vondelpark and had spent every day with since, I headed out of Amsterdam on my European adventure. So much for EurailPasses and itineraries!

comments.name: Patrick Purcell
comments.body: I live in England. I have had InterRail passes in 1979, 1981 (aged 18 and 20) and in 2023, 2023 and 2025 (aged 62 and 64). Fantastic then, fantastic now. Second Class then, First Class now. Unbelievable value in expensive rail countries like Norway Switzerland and the UK (where I live so I cannot use it here). If you have ever wondered about getting one...do it. You will not regret it. A pleasant 2-3 hour journey and you are in a different country with a different language and culture. Enjoy!

comments.name: Guido
comments.body:
Eurail was never just word
It was always/instantly a verb
For an era that knew no bounds
Had no gobs of cash or eats
Bound and determined to discover the world of Frommer travel
Where the journey and the destination smoothly/simply blended into one steel vehicle for unknown/unexpected pleasures
Timeless
Priceless
Seamless

It's about time that we imported it back here
What a wonderful place
What a perfect time
To start along the 5,500-mile borderless border
between us and Canada

All Aboard!

comments.name: Times Rita
comments.body: Europe on $5 a Day and a Eurail pass. That was the rite of passage for so many of us in the early 70s. And of course, Amesterdam was the hub, with Canadian patches on Americans' backpacks. So sad to see the name change. So sad to learn that there are fewer overnight trains.

comments.name: Clay
comments.body:
One of the great joys of a Eurail pass vacation was accidentally taking the wrong train.

I'm headed to Pisa instead of Milan? Sure, why not? 

Never any regrets.

comments.name: Amos
comments.body: When I started out of Israel in 1972, rail travel was too expensive for me. Hitchhiked all over Europe for the next 3 years. I don't even comprehend now how I did all that on almost no money. But I was young then.

comments.name: GT
comments.body:
Christmas 1977 my dad gave me and my best friend a 4 week first class Eurail pass. We did nothing but plan until high school graduation came and we were free. Eurail was also used on the ferry system and provided other discounts. The FC pass all but guaranteed a seat or sleeper spot if the train had them. Not all that unusual for USA kids to have the FC pass.

We spent 2 weeks in the UK and used the Eurail pass for the first  time (starting the 4 week clock) on the ferry to France. It did not work in the UK back then and Britrail was not worth getting. The last day of the pass found us leaving Brindisi (Italy) on a ferry to the port of Athens. The popular book at the time was Europe on $5 a day  ... we averaged $20 most days staying in hostels and budget places. I do remember getting to Paros (Greece) after a week island hopping with $250 US in my pouch. Had prepaid the return ferry ticket to Athens and one to NYC on Olympic Air.  After a full week in Paros I landed in NY with $80. 

It was a life changing, confidence building summer. I never lost the travel bug ... went to grad school in Europe and became a PCV in Africa. Have worked all over the world. It also strengthened the bond with my friend that has stayed with us all these years ...

articles.title: Eurail, the Longtime Savior of Shoestring Backpackers, Ditches Its Name
articles.summary: The flexible train ticket is rebranding itself as the Interrail Pass. For many travelers, the old name evokes a bygone era of freewheeling European travel.

comments.name: Cab
comments.body: To me the greatest long term impact of 9/11 was the Patriot Act which established the infrastructure necessary for the United States to become a police state; a process that continues today and will haunt future generations. The loss, the trauma, and the fear generated by the attack has also emotionally locked the American soul into a trajectory that will carry us further into what promises to be an erosion of our freedoms in deference to a legitimate need for security and safety. Phrases like "Never Again" or "Never Forget" carry a double meaning. A 9/11 type of event must never be repeated or forgotten; but, I fear that we may never again truly be as free as we thought ourselves to be on 9/10.

comments.name: Mitten Dweller
comments.body:
Friday Sept. 14 I and a coworker drove home  from Hartford, CT to Michigan, we had flights booked but the airport was pretty chaotic.  At our stops along the way we experienced that American Family feeling.  We were so polite, friendly, courteous.  We had all  BEEN through something and were on our best behavior because it felt right.

In the months to follow the American response to Sept 11 unfolded.  I observed, horrified, the bipartisan approval of The Patriot Act. The frenzy in the aftermath of a national calamity was used to shave more of our Constitutional Rights away.  Also, in my opinion, the lies perpetrated to soften up the gullible public to accept and support the reasons for invading Iraq.  Any goodwill toward America resulting from 9-11 was squandered as far as I was concerned.  I’m no apologist for Saddam Hussein, and he needed to be gone.  Only don’t lie to me and the world about the justification for doing it.   We’ve learned nothing and have not improved one bit.

comments.name: kc
comments.body: Had Al Gore been President then, he likely would have used the overwhelming feeling of patriotism in the USA to shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy.  That was his passion and it is the only time in our history that I believe our citizens would have been willing.  9/11 did bring us together - if only we could have had a leader to channel that energy into something positive.

comments.name: Stoic in the 314
comments.body: What really changed us was the way in which we responded to 9/11. We have been at war ever since, and except for hunting down OBL, have done little to improve our standing in the world. A prime example is the global refugee crisis.

comments.name: Oci
comments.body:
Well, this is tremendous obviously. Still, 9/11 was the end of something — far too on-the-nose to miss. The beginning of the fall, the falling of the towers, the insertion into our little bubble of tidings from the rest of the planet and everything going on there.
I missed 9/11 — I was living without television or the web in a tiny town in the countryside of a foreign country. But when I returned home two months later it was to an already much changed America, and while we’ve moved on now, we have never gone and are never going back.

comments.name: HOUDINI
comments.body: One of the better essays I've read. With 25 yr. hindsight, the polar opposites of 45 & 47 attack and return are well stated. Yes, the day was sparkling clear, the wind crisp and it changed my view of many things.

comments.name: Donald
comments.body:
9/11 was an attack by mideast elements against a nation that had constantly interfered in the region for the benefit of Israel. A place where we had no borders and no history. Twenty five years later we are still at war in the region with Arab states for the benefit of Israel. This toxic relationship has endured because of the complicity of money, media, and deceit . 

We learn only recently that Israel know of the planned Jan 7 attack and let it happen. It was their Pearl Harbor event that justified brutality in return. Another land grab with "security " at its core. The corruption of history and the paranoia in the American mind is what brought us here. The fever is still with us but the carrier was not IRAQ/IRAN it was Israel. That disease is very much still with us. Only now, to some , do we find out current war , started by Israel will be paid for by America.

comments.name: Mary C
comments.body:
Imagine the world if the Supreme Court had not interfered with the 2000 election and Gore had been president?
Bush ignored Clinton's warnings about bin Laden, so maybe 9/11 would never have happened. 
Certainly, the aftermath would have been very different. 
No Iraq war for one thing.

articles.title: Did 9/11 Really Change Everything?
articles.summary: Were the terrorist attacks that day the end of an idyllic era? The beginning of our current dystopia? Or just a middle chapter?

comments.name: G. Toher
comments.body: I was living in Mineola that year and watched the second plane fly into the second tower. My first words? “OMG! This is no accident. “ I too will spend this anniversary like Mr. Feinberg, quiet, alone, and contemplative. I am sure we will not be the only two.

comments.name: ellienyc
comments.body: I always thought it was disgusting the way the airline lobbyists threatened Congress with that cockamamie story the airlines would go bankrupt and millions would lose their jobs unless they used our tax money to pay the 911 families off. Then they pulled a similar stunt during COVID. And what have the airlines given us in return?

comments.name: kathy
comments.body: Thank you, sir for doing a thankless job. Of course you made mistakes, how could you not when working with unprecedented circumstances. I hope and pray you can find some joy in retirement

comments.name: Elmy ĥ
comments.body: Can you imagine if trump had been in charge then? He'd put himself in charge of the payouts.

comments.name: John Manhattan
comments.body: As this article commented about a 2nd cup of coffee, I was one block away, having not had my morning coffee, so I went into a "deli" on Liberty St and was at the register about to pay when "something" happened. The North Tower came down.  I was safe inside. All thanks to needing my morning coffee.

comments.name: FreewayAs
comments.body: He sounds like a virtuous, honest man of integrity who did the best he could in a horrific situation. Sleep well Mr. Feinberg you were there when America needed you and you did what you could which is all any of us can do.

comments.name: Dean C. Rowan
comments.body:
I can't fathom having to have assumed the responsibility he assumed. It would have been, as they say, "above my pay grade." 

However, time is not the enemy. Time just is. I want to say that the enemy is the enemy, but that opens the door to all sorts of malignant ideological assertions that America, post-9/11, has had to endure, thanks to our cynical, craven, self-interested leadership.

comments.name: JH
comments.body: The trouble with life is you think you have more time than you do.

articles.title: The Man Who Approved 9/11 Victims’ Checks Paid a Price
articles.summary: Kenneth Feinberg says the nearly three years he spent running the Sept. 11 compensation fund changed his life view forever.

comments.name: Canadien
comments.body:
Our Canadian family of four often read the comments as we finds most Americans are so different from Canadians. Not meant as a dig, but you truly are different, as such, we learn from your postings. If our trade war gets uglier, our family would be willing to give sanctuary to the following NYT posters who seem sane:
1. Socrates, who hails from beautiful downtown Verona in the state of Mary Land. His posting are always so wise.
2. Marge Kellogg who lives somewhere in America's middle western states. Her husband is British so he would feel at home in Canada. Canada, and British Columbia especially, is chock a block with Brits, Scots, and Irish. We live in horse country on Vancouver Island so that may make our Marge happy.
3. ManhattanWilliam. However old he is, he is wise beyond his years. Our son enjoys his postings.
4. Passion for Peaches. Her quirkiness would make her an ideal Canadian. And we have peaches growing in the interior of British Columbia.
5. There are so many sane Americans that live in the city of New York that post and that we embrace. Before I was married I had a grand holiday in New York City. I went to ALL five boroughs. Loved the Bronx. Very kind people. Ate food from buggy carts that I could not pronounce but were very tasty. The Bronx Zoo was great. Could not get into Yankee Stadium but did have a Nathan's. 
If you can get out of the US, get out while you can. It will only get worse in America. We hope and pray your midterms are bloodless.

comments.name: John
comments.body: Perhaps the fine Gander residents could invite Ambassador Hoekstra to become an honorary Newfoundlander and offer to have him screeched-in.

comments.name: Lynn
comments.body: Thank you Gander and thank you Canada. The majority of us stand with you and will forever be grateful for your support and kindnesses. As someone recently reminded me..”He, too, shall pass”.

comments.name: MPage
comments.body: Many years ago, I spent two weeks traveling in Newfoundland, a young woman alone. I was staying in a little inn in Rock Harbor for a few nights. On my second night, the waitress in the little restaurant noticed I was alone. She invited me to have dinner at her house the next night, and her charming husband took me out on his boat to watch the sunset with a glass of “screech”. His Newfie accent was so thick I could barely understand him but oh my, I hung on his every word. This was 1989. What wonderful people, what a memory!

comments.name: Marian, NYC

I remain deeply grateful to Canadians for what they did on 9/11 as well as what they did in rescuing Americans in Iran in 1979.  I am deeply ashamed of Donald Trump.

comments.name: Deborah
comments.body: I know myself well, and if - God forbid - 9/11 happened tomorrow I would still react the same way Canada did on 9/11. Canadians are better human beings than this administration would like us to be and I believe many Americans would do the same for us!

comments.name: Aaron Of Gladstone

comments.name: Deborah

comments.name: Steph K
comments.body: If you want more detailed breakdowns of auto tune in music, watch the Wings of Pegasus YT channel. Fil (host) gives great insight into how the technology is being used.

comments.name: Frank Quigley
comments.body: I play the drum kit. High intermediate skill. Have taken YEARS of lessons and practice every day. I play local jazz jams and will start playing with a guitarist as "The Coconuts". (Jimmy Buffett, Alan Jackson, Zac Brown Band, Guy Clark . . .) I see guys playing sith super-expensive Roland electronic sets. These kits mask every flaw. Make a poker sound like Phil Collins. And the drummers are all "showy". I don't get it. Need true acoustical instruments including vocals in order to truly communicate and connect. I work on timing, tempo, precision, syncopation, dynamics - and swinging it. Why wouldn't anyone just want to actually master their craft?

comments.name: Me
comments.body: I was in the SNL studio audience years ago. The musical act performed and his voice was horrible. Went home watched the performance and his voice was pitch perfect.

comments.name: R
comments.body: You can't sustain dancing and singing for a time without getting at least a little breathless and I never hear that.

comments.name: Bradley Bleck
comments.body: I’d rather have flawed reality.

comments.name: LBJr
comments.body:
Wings of Pegasus (on YouTube) is where to go if you want more auto-tune sleuthing.  I'm a bit miffed that the author of this article did not mention Fil (or is it Phil... I can't remember).  

Auto-tune.  Self-driving cars.  MAGA-face.  People who use A.I. for anything creative.  They are a type.  From my point of view they are people who really don't want to live life, they want a technology to live life for them.  Much of our culture is obsessed with output at the expense of self-fulfillment.  Learning how to sing is soooooo much more satisfying than having auto-tune do most of the work.  But, the auto-tuners don't really want accomplishment, they want "likes" and "thumbs-up" and "left-swipes" and shallow popularity.  Our consumer-based world rewards this non-existence.  Clavicular?  Trump?  Travis Scott?  Most any Real Housewife?  Truly pathetic.

comments.name: jeff clapp
comments.body: It really is sick. A.i., auto-tune, robots everywhere. Sad, sad. What people will stoop to, due to their own insecurities. American actors sound like they're on auto tune now--and they look like mannequins. No warts, no wrinkles. Perfect teeth. And bad actin. I watch TV shows from other parts of the world, and I have no interest in machine-made pop music. It sounds dead.

comments.name: Jon
comments.body:
Interesting that the late 90s were the real advent of this.  I say that because the 1990s were the time that stretching and shrieking and torturing every single syllable to death and beyond became the gold standard in vocal performance (personally, I found it impossible to sit through, like every pop song was suddenly an overwrought national anthem rendition).  

That probably intimidated some musicians who just wanted to, you know, sing songs. Respect to those who carried on with genuine self-expression.  I assure you, none of my favorites are fantasists about their own gifts, or cowards about their limitations thereof.

comments.name: Brian P. Kalfus
comments.body: It’s refreshing to read about how others have as much difficulty understanding dialogue as I do. Sometimes when I watch a movie a second time with subtitles after seeing it without in a theater, it’s as if it’s an entirely different movie. Plots can sometimes be complicated, and misunderstanding even one sentence can lose me entirely. (Sometimes I can’t hear dialogue because of rude audience members, but that’s a topic for another time.) I still need to see Saving Private Ryan with subtitles, even though depicting the chaotic communication on D-Day was the point.

comments.name: Frank Beans
comments.body: Modern film, tv and increasingly live theater have surrenderred the art form to sound design. The use of sound to manipulate our experience of those mediums has become intolerable to anyone who regularly also watches old masters of those forms. When your ears are overwhlemed constantly there's no room for you brain to process that the story and artistry is otherwise vapid.

comments.name: Peter Magnan
comments.body: I started using captions while watching the first season of Luther.  The characters all came from a different part of Britain, and each one spoke in their own dialect.  While everyone spoke English, the captions helped to make everyone comprehensible.

comments.name: Alan
comments.body: I find the dialogue in many television programs and movies almost  unintelligible. Extreme teeth rattling base or actors speaking as to cover up that they have forgotten their lines seems to be the norm. With the exception of radio and televised sporting events can you hear good audio fidelity. Ironic the announcers at a golf tournament are clearly understood in hushed whispers. The lack of sound quality cannot be excused for the artifice of making the scene more real. Even Humphrey Bogart can be understood clearly compared to what we are forced to decipher.

comments.name: East Of Cicero

comments.name: Andy

comments.name: Shantonu Basu
comments.body: The best way to understand Shakespeare is to watch his plays with the subtitles on. It's like reading his plays but with better comprehension. Or so I have found. You can "read" all of his plays in about six months without too much effort. So glad for captions!

comments.name: Susie
comments.body: Who can live richly without words in front of their eyes?  Subtitles are just an extension of all those cereal boxes I read as a kid.

articles.title: Who Says Reading Is Dead?
articles.summary: Young people are streaming videos with captions and sound.

comments.name: Aodhán Ó Cuinn
comments.body:
Why are they so slow in San Francisco in imposing rent controls? It seems very late in the day to be making an issue out of housing costs now. 

Vienna, Austria, by the way, has the most exceptional public policy on housing with public servants and low-income workers being guaranteed housing. 

Under the Wien Social Housing model, half the city's residents (220,000 apartments) live in subsidised or municipal apartments. Another 200,000 homes are built by housing cooperatives with government support. Critically, Vienna places people of different income levels in the same buildings. This stops poor neighborhoods from forming.

Vienna is a global success story in housing, much like Finland is in education. Is any US city or state emulating it?

comments.name: Bill
comments.body: Sounds to me if you have an apartment you can afford be grateful. If it has mold, some bugs, noisy neighbors, and you aren’t happy…MOVE!

comments.name: Em's daughter
comments.body: I am surprised there is no mention of the corporate takeover of thousands of homes and rental properties. The shareholders need to be fed the profits from the ever increasing rents hell or high water. Also I just did a search on Air B & B in San Francisco and there were 1000 vacation rentals listed. That adds to the shortages of available living spaces for residents too. This is happening everywhere.

comments.name: John C
comments.body: Someone please explain to me why individual people have to subsidize other individuals when society want to provide a social good?

comments.name: James
comments.body:
Incredibly frustrating there isn't a single time on this agenda to actually build more housing. Just another set of bandaids.

I'm actually shocked to see the number of NYT comments blaming this on tech or mocking landlords. Just completely letting our politicians off the hook for their failure to build housing.

comments.name: Rick Girling
comments.body: @Longtime SFer I’ve lived in SF for over 50 years. Rents and housing prices are stratospheric. My two sons and one girlfriend all in their late 20s with good paying jobs live with me and my wife because there is indeed a crisis. Billionaires like Mayor Lurie and his friends have no clue! Why would anyone oppose Proposition I (as Lurie has) for dedicating funds that have been already been collected to building affordable housing unless they are pals with the real estate and tech bros who make out like bandits as housing prices skyrocket? We need a mayor who cares about the working class like Mamdani here!

comments.name: Elizabeth
comments.body:
While there have been some green shoots in willingness to build housing (mostly forced by changes to state law), the city remains far too willing to entertain efforts that block housing or make it more expensive. Just this week, even as the mayor endorsed many of these laudable measures to protect tenants, the planning department and one supervisor pushed forward a completely excessive historic district proposal for the Castro that would provide a blueprint for other neighborhoods to form their own historic districts, add a lot of restrictions, review, and cost to any sort of new housing development, and make the city even less accessible to anyone but the rich. (Part of the rationale for the district is that Eureka Valley was the first 'streetcar suburb' in SF as it expanded out of downtown. What are we even doing here?)

If elected officials and the planning department are serious about making this a place that a diverse population can live, they need to stop trying to overengineer everything or freeze the building stock. Just get out of the way and let people build housing.

comments.name: Nubby Shober
comments.body: URBANISM is the answer. Building 5-8 story multi-use buildings close to subway, rail, and major bus hubs. Stores on ground floor; offices on 2nd & 3rd floors; and apartments above. To create walkable, affordable neighborhoods in close proximity to mass transit.

For mote than a year now, I have refused to buy Treasuries; I no longer fund meaningless wars, corruption, and an unaccountable oligarchy.

comments.name: E. Henry Schoenberger

First, objective critical thinking reveals that inflation is a ruse to cover up greed, notwithstanding protestations to the contrary.  It is a mere conclusion that cannot be backed up by facts if you analyze the assumptions which are naked assertions.  Not talking about the time before greed was regulated.

And, it is imperative to recall that decades ago it was held by economists that to control inflation took a combination of monetary policy (interest rates) with fiscal policy (tax rates).

To lower taxes and raise interest rates at the same time, or not increase tax rates and interest rates in counter intuitive; ie, will not work.   

Hence, to raise interest rates is like shooting BBs at tanks. How much better would it be to go back to regulating greed? RGA - Regulate Greed Again.

comments.name: Rich W
comments.body:
Article perpetuates the myth that when bond prices decline, it does not affect an investor who holds a bond to maturity, while an investor who owns bonds in a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund, will lose money.

Individual Bond: You lose paper value initially. Over time, that loss shrinks until the bond reaches maturity and pays out at par value.

Bond Mutual Fund: You lose Net Asset Value  initially. Over time, that loss is neutralized by the compounding effect of higher dividend distributions as the fund rolls into new, higher-yielding securities.

It's the same.

comments.name: HSK

comments.name: Dead Rabbits
comments.body:
Not to confuse people more but is the bond market is pricing in something worse—Stagflation.   

Look at the 2yr-30y yield differential. It has tightened this month from 110 basis points to 70 basis points.  

Typically this widens with inflation expectations increasing.  Here however it’s going the other way.  High short  term rates, high long term rates but less so because of low GDP fears.

comments.body:
Those in the Northeast with homes still heated by heating oil are facing a very expensive winter. Especially those on fixed or limited incomes. Likely too late in the year to those who can afford it - and have a house/residence setup that is suitable for conversion - to start the process to switch to split level heat pumps. Maine has long had a state supported heat pump conversion program. But has a ways to go.
If the federal government does not step up, hope the New England and NY states can expand their assistance programs to help with the high home heating bills. Will be a rough winter for many in the Northeast who use heating oil.

comments.location: East End Of The Milky Way
comments.body:
That price still does not include all costs incurred, not even close. 
We should include all costs, then the price per gallon will triple, and that will result in real change.

comments.name: hen3ry
comments.body:
What worries me is that a lot of prices will not come down even if the price of oil does.  To use a trivial example, during the pandemic, the size of rolls of toilet paper decreased.  Ergo the price increased.  The pandemic ended.  The toilet paper rolls didn't return to their previous size.  The same can be said for package sizes of food, clothing, etc.  I remember when a regular container of yogurt was 8 oz.  I remember when we could buy a five pound bag of sugar or, even earlier, a full pound of coffee at a reasonable price.  Now we have four pound bags of sugar and 12 or 10 oz. sizes of coffee.  These sizes will not change.

Housing prices started a steady increase in the 1980s.  There is far less affordable decent housing than needed.  Very little has been done to improve the situation.  Wages began to stagnate in 1973.  We're still suffering the effects of that.  Fewer and fewer employees are protected by a union.  It's the Republican and corporate dream:  the ability to fire, abuse, and underpay employees at will.  

My point is that it's not all going to end if the price of oil comes down.  Most of it remains.

comments.body: The Holocaust stands out as something that I can never find humor in. I’ve never seen The Producers  and I stay away from movies that portray Hitler in a humorous light. And I don’t find anything funny about catastrophes, murder, or child abusers. While I am a big fan of Louis CK ( I find it interesting that he isn’t mentioned in this article) whenever he finds humor in any of these subjects, I can’t go there with him.

comments.body: When is too soon? It took nearly a decade following JFK's assassination for the National Lampoon Magazine to parody that November 22, 1963 event that left Americans traumatized. Too soon?

comments.name: Jennu
comments.body: Irony and trolling devalue public discourse, especially when constant. Unfortunately, it does not appear to be a particularly reversible trend, maybe because of the relationship to entertainment.  But skepticism and contradictory presentation often become formulaic and wears us down.   Making fun of everything begins to mean nothing- which is the point in certain styles of political discourse.  Voices for clarity and logic get drowned out.  We need a reliable forum that limits the winking and nudging.

comments.name: Noah
comments.body:
One of the few things that gives me hope for our country is how many genuinely funny people there are out there in “the comments.” True, you often have to wade through some of the worst of humanity along the way, but there are quite a few gems, too. 

I believe a sense of humor, and gallows humor in particular, is absolutely necessary for our collective and individual survival. I’m not sure if gallows humor would be considered irony, though. 

Bill Maher wasn’t being funny when he said the terrorists were brave (Maher is rarely being funny extemporaneously or otherwise.) He was voicing a controversial opinion, which unfortunately the internet and social media allows too many other blowhards who think they are funny to do on a never-ending basis. However, the dumpster fire of bad takes that is the internet and social media shouldn’t be confused with humor or irony.

And thankfully, AI has absolutely no sense of humor, so it may be the one way to tell the difference between what’s real and what’s artificial going forward.

comments.name: A geologist
comments.body:
The article nicely notes benefits for "shoulder" off season October/November travel. Of course fewer people, less crowds, better weather, less heat/extreme heat.

Let me remind this shifting pattern is not tangential to climate change but a result of.

October into November travel would not be a persistent norm were not warmer weather conditions shifting beyond usual seasonal   temperatures into later months.

Pls bear with me.
Let's look at beautiful Moab--at the Moab station average (avg) July temps. 2024 July daily temps were 95°F to 100°F. Hot, dangerous.

Since 1893 average (avg) high July temps rose by degrees.

1893 July avg is 93.8°F
You don't get 100°F avgs highs until 1934 at 100.7°F.
All years after 1921 are above 95°F except 2015.
All years after 1941 are above 97°F except 2015.
All years after 1944 are above 98°F except  1955/1965/1983/1987/2015.
All years after... you see where this us going.
The coolest July was 1897 at 87.8°F
After 1951 there are 29 years with avg July temps > 100°F. 
Only two year > 100 from 1983 to 1950.

October average highs warm but not as much & remain comfortable.

Yes, there are fluctuations but trends are clear and persistent. Per the FDA growing zones are shifting north, growing seasons are longer at both ends.

Since the 1980s we learned heat domes are the summer norm, roaming the hemisphere and circling the arctic, adding excessive summer heat.

In simple terms, this is climate change. Favorable travel seasons are also shifting.

comments.name: Bea

Several years ago, while leading marketing for a division of a multi-national company (top 20% of Fortune 500), I represented marketing across all divisions to define our Ai policies with Legal. We elected to prohibit use of open Ai platforms, for fear the tools would absorb our IP.  We also prohibited use of open generative Ai for the creation of content for fear we might inadvertently plagiarize another party’s IP. 

Instead, we opted to use a closed tools that we could train ourselves, by feeding reems of our own content into the platforms, and then, leveraging the proprietary model to generate content (such as marketing materials, web copy, etc.).

Two issues: 1) policy is one thing, but from a practical perspective, it’s impossible to police more than 100k employees’ use of AI in a world where they all have access to their own home computer and mobile phone, 2) the self-trained AI model’s output was abysmal. I’m still not sure whether the issue was a matter of “garbage in, garbage out”,  if we simply didn’t have the expertise to tweak the outputs, if we needed more than the 200k historical training documents, or if the tech providers deliberately make the closed systems inferior to the open ones, on the basis that it’s the best way to convert companies to the open ones, thereby gaining access to the data.

What began as a fascinating learning experience ended as one of the more frustrating projects in my career. But it didn’t stop the ongoing demand that we leverage ai!

comments.name: Cynthia
comments.body: A lot of AI articles in this paper, including the Broad and Metz piece from yesterday, minimize the risks and take a much more hopeful tone, and they've done so for several years. But the fact is that AI isn't surprising anybody by becoming more and more benign and easier to control as time passes. Every passing month the news is that it's harder to control, that it is doing more and more unexpected things, and that its capabilities are growing faster than anyone predicted and farther than anyone can explain. Given all that, doomsaying seems a wiser approach than hopeful optimism. Hope for the best, maybe, but prepare for the worst. Our government has no appetite for that. It seems to be preparing for nothing these days except for how to disrupt the upcoming election. I don't agree with Broad and Metz. I guess we'll see.

comments.name: Jon Yaffe
comments.body:
The idea of a safe and responsible AI contains a fundamental challenge to our current values regarding privacy.
If your job is fulfilling the requests of people - which of course means people of all ranges of intelligence, maturity, mental health and who knows what other factors - then it's not enough to simply grant requests as asked. 
If a seven year-old asks how to build an IED, do you simply hand over a set of intructions? I'm going to go out on a limb here, and say 'No'. 
My point is that AIs, like any party asked for input, need to know the answer, not cheat to get the answer, AND know the  persons asking. What are their intentions, their capabilities, their ability to honor reasonable codes of cunduct, etc?
There's no way to do this properly without having extensive background information on users, and vetting them based on a far-reaching set of criteria. 
This will make privacy advocates go crazy, just as it will make all the people who simply want AIs to leverage their own intentions without regard for the ethics of those intentions crazy as well.
Sorry, but working this through is the price we need to pay. AI's will force us to truly grow up, or perish.

How Did a Heart Drug With So Much Promise Fall So Flat?

It's disappointing but the truth is a very low percentage of drugs  pass muster during clinical trials.  It's not surprising, but it's sure frustrating that after all these years of research we still have such a long way to go to understand heart disease and so many other ailments.

comments.name: Rick
comments.body: Cardiologist here.  Manipulation of the various components of a "lipid panel" have had mixed results.  High LDL and low HDL are both associated with increased adverse cardiovascular events.  Lowering LDL effectively lowers that risk.  Raising HDL, it would stand to reason, should also be beneficial.  Unfortunately, real life doesn't always cooperate...  Drugs that raise HDL have not been shown to confer any meaningful benefit.  Looks like LP(a) is traveling down the same road.

comments.name: SBS
comments.body:
It would be unfortunate if scientists completely abandon the lp(a) hypothesis even if the Lilly and Amgen trials fail, because my understanding is that ALL of the major ongoing trials focus on treating older patients who have either (a) already had heart attacks or (b) haven't yet but do already have diagnosed cardiovascular disease.  (The recent trial was only (a); some of the others include (b), which they refer to as primary prevention even though it's not truly a healthy population.) What I badly want to know (as a high-lp(a) patient) is whether and when any company plans to invest in testing the thesis floated in this article: that lowering lp(a) over a long period of time, beginning *before* there is plaque buildup, does have clinical benefits even if doesn't if you wait to a later stage.  True primary prevention, that is. I would sign up for that trial! 

My understanding is that the companies' current focus is basically practical/financial: when you start a trial on younger, asymptomatic people, the baseline risk is low at first and it takes much longer before you have answers. Even so, the long-term payoff if it does work could be great--not just for patients but, financially, for the company that finds a drug people will take for many decades, perhaps even starting in childhood.  And if a study starts with cohorts, say, in their 50s, 40s, and 30s, it might well have usable results for the oldest cohort in not too long.  When will someone do this?

He died over 20 years ago, after he wrote “Cholesterol Is Not The Culprit.” He started researching heart attacks by asking coroners for the arteries of heart attack victims. He found that hydrogenated cholesterol lodged in arteries was the primary cause of heart attacks. Fats kept in broilers to fry donuts, chicken and French fries became hydrogenated after continued use, so to put it succinctly, it’s the fries, not the hamburgers.

comments.name: sleeve

As a Registered Dietitian, I can say with certainty that cardiologists have very routinely gotten nutrition flat out wrong.  I hold them largely responsible for the obesity epidemic in the US with their recommendations for low fat diets which lead people to believe starches and sugars were okay.  They also got it terribly wrong when they recommended very low sodium intakes for blood pressure.  As you may recall, patients died on that study of diets with less than 1500 mgs of sodium daily.  What they failed to realize is that renin, produced by the kidneys, is a rescue hormone that will be released to increase blood pressure in response to low serum sodium.  
I firmly believe they are in the wrong about cholesterol with the true culprits likely being  carnitine and lecithin……so close, since they recommended decreasing red meat and eggs the major sources of those respectively, but they misidentified the actual problematic causes which seem to occur via our gut microbiota, which can produce heart attack inducing compounds.   
Nutrition is highly complex and best understood by people who have studied holistically instead of piecemeal to make it conform to their various off-base theories over the decades when they were basically allowed to unilaterally call the shots.

The article misses the most effective method for making cold water acceptable for most:  the gradual mixing in the shower from warm to cold. Done that way the transition is easy. Hate the thought of even a tiny bit of cold? Spend a few minutes -and a few more as necessary- of gradually dialing down the temp so you just notice each degree change, without feeling hammered by them. This builds confidence/reduces fear.
I've done this every morning for years and see no reason (and still don't want) to shock my system by going straight into cold right away. 

The practice does have benefits for me. It's a great every day way to wake up more fully, makes me much more resistant to seasonal weather extremes both hot and cold, and noticeably improves circulation and overall qi energy flow. 

Cost is nothing, no travel time involved, and doing this every day in your own shower is much more effective than a semi-regular or occasional trip to a river or facility. And the more you do it, the easier it gets, and you eventually even look forward to it. Start now -summer cold water from the tap is far less cold than it will be come January...

Do this mornings only, and never when sick or when fighting off a cold, etc.

I lived in Los Angeles and at some point decided I would volunteer to teach people to read; after all, as an aspiring screenwriter, it seemed a way to ensure an audience and elevate opportunities for other citizens at the same time.
The only proto-internet organization that was easy to find was a group on Hollywood Boulevard. I volunteered and went in for 'training.'
After noting that the books in the lending library were all L Ron Hubbard and other weirdness designed to indoctrinate rather than teach literacy, I was bothered.
After being made to sit and watch several odd 45 min. movies about the meaning of language before I could even begin to teach what I actually knew, I walked out. It wasn't that I was ignorant, it was that the narrative line was that 'current' language/idioms were only used by idiots, and that we all should revert our word usage to early 19th century usage.
In other words, the video was telling us all that words have specific meanings, and those meanings are frozen in time from a place that serves the Scientologists.
I walked away. 
I'll never look at Scientologists the same way.
So since then I've been OK with the idea that Beck's music is fine ear candy, but essentially hollow and devoid of any tangible depth or essential human meaning. 
He is a hollow man, making balsa constructions, no matter how entertaining, for a future that will eventually crush them into dust.
Yay.

comments.name: Aristotle
comments.body:
"China’s “growth was fueled by unfair trade practices,” Piyush Goyal, India’s commerce minister, said last year. “This growth happened at the cost of fair play.”

China's entry into the world economy created a false hope that it would eventually look more like a Western country, w/ little interest in asserting itself as a rival to the U.S. Instead China integrated into the world economy under its own rules, bringing it's own distinctive values and institutions, and its own national interest to the global stage. In China public-private collaboration plays an important role in its economic policies. That this violates tenets of unfettered capitalism that underscores free-market neoliberalism is its only sin.  In truth, no country better illustrates the benefits of public-private collaboration than China.

comments.name: Eddie B.

Although the pretext is a BRICS meeting, but Xi's visit to India is not entirely unexpected.  This is indeed a critical moment in the history of both countries and this visit can prove to be extremely important. In terms of its significance, I put it as high as Richard Nixon's visit to China in 1972.

Americans should not be surprised to see much closer relationships between China and India in 2027. This visit could be followed by with China offering India much needed financial support for its large infrastructure projects. 

While the US is deep in the hole thanks to its $40 Trillion debt, China has a lot of money to spread around. And they will do that strategically, with a long-term view of China’s place in the world.

Indeed !

I know many people who have revealed that a great deal of the enjoyment of travel is the research and planning that goes into creating a memorable trip.

They have related that the most pleasurable day of their travel is the first day of the trip " looking forward" to the fruit of their planning. 

Of course this runs counter to all the aphorisms that teach human beings to " live in the moment "  

" "Do not dwell in the past, do not dream of the future, concentrate the mind on the present moment." — Buddha"

All of which is to elaborate that human beings are unique creatures with a wide array of attributes and foibles that fall along a bell shaped curve.

comments.name: Bigger Picture

I think that I’m like a lot of other people.  I used to enjoy buying things because they made me happy.

But as an old guy, I really don’t need anything unless it’s to replace something that’s broken or worn out.

Nowadays I satisfy my dopamine hit by going to the supermarket to search for bargains on items that I routinely buy (but never to buy something just because it’s on sale.)

I us my smartphone to compare prices to items found on-line.  Sometimes the supermarket price is much lower than on-line prices.

I get my dopamine hit, get out of the house for awhile when the supermarket isn’t crowded and save money.

comments.name: TMC
comments.body: That Maisel captured the essence of a new jazz movement in a single image is perfect. "Kind of Blue" was all about the modality of sound, explored and developed in that 1959 Davis/Evans collaboration. Maisel's color photography was the visual equivalent. So many of his photos have a sort of layered mood caused by colors abstracted from their context, set against each other, saturated vs muted.

comments.name: Lorin Duckman
comments.body: No one like him . Saw dignity in everything; made you see it too. Not anyone who studied,worked or knew him will forget him or his voice.

comments.name: JP
comments.body: I spent 10 days and 9 US cities traveling with Jay for an annual report shoot, a joy and a profound experience in the presence of an artist. But very savvy in business and corporate ways, as his commercial success showed. Visiting him in NYC in his bank/studio/home, trying to figure out my own career, his personality and generosity of spirit was ever present. He was so curious and open to life, to seeing. And funny. Standing on the front steps to his Bowery building on day, he asked me, “Do you think I’m eccentric?” I laughed. “Jay, you live in a bank.” He was so much of a time and place, a figure in photography, New York, no doubt known and friend to many, but first and foremost  a wonderful human.

comments.name: Ed Greenberg
comments.body: A true Damyon Runyon character.  One of a kind and there will never be another.  He was at his best while smoking cigars with his buddies, aspiring photographers, philosophers and comedians.  A quintessential New Yorker and likely that last of the breed. Funny, wise with a touch of Mel Brooks. The sad end to an era.

comments.name: John McD.
comments.body: As great as Jay was as a photographer he was an even better man. He influenced and helped so many up-and-coming photographers, including me. I was inspired by his work, to be sure. But I was also inspired by his kindness and generosity, his sense of humor and his wonderful character. He was a very special man. RIP, dear Jay. Your memory will always be a blessing.

And even though I remember 9/11 and its aftermath vividly, I was actually more moved by the simple, yet divine, memorial pools with the names of the dead than by all the museum displays.  That's where all the sadness and love really persist.

The fact that, in spite of fires, wars, earthquakes and impacts, NO steel high rise structure has ever collapsed with the force that took down these three towers although only two were even hit by airplanes.  We have all seen dozens of steel towers collapse but in EVERY case the “implosions” were caused by the carefully engineered placement of explosives and their systematic ignition. This type of implosion represents a perfect example of the three demolitions that we witnessed on 911, yet, like the Epstein scandal, our media is careful to keep the truth carefully covered up.  The United States is clearly not the country that we have been led to believe it is.  It never will be until its citizens are given the TRUTH that they deserve.

comments.name: Carla
comments.body:
As a retired NYC elementary teacher, I wanted to show students that history is stories that live with people.  Everybody of a certain age remembers where they were when they heard that President John F. Kennedy had been shot. EachNovember as we went off to the Thanksgiving break I'd assign students to ask family members where they were when President Kennedy was assassinated. They came back with stories from all over the world and an interest in how that event impacted people.

In 2000, I stopped asking that question because the students had their own shared story of an event that lived with them.  I hope that they share those stories and their grandchildren ask, 'Where were you when 9/11 happened?'

comments.name: Lydia
comments.body: During my second visit to the Museum, I was offended by people who were photographing in areas clearly marked no photography. After stepping in front of these rude visitors, I paused on the third level to collect my thoughts and exited the Museum. Be a good American when you visit this hallowed space.

comments.name: zb
comments.body:
The structural engineers for the world trade center was Worthington, Skilling, Helle and Jackson.  I found no reference to them at the museum's Website.   A friend of mine was their on site structural engineer during the construction of the world trade center.  He gave years of his life, making sure it was built right.  Without their unique design, more likely than not
Both buildings would have collapsed almost immediately, and thousands of more lives would have been lost and yet, there appears to be no mention of them at the museum. 

Thousands of lives of soldiers, and tens, or even hundreds of thousands of innocents died in the aftermath of our effort to bring justice.  Thousands more who helped us in that effort were abandoned to their own terrible fate after we left.

Dig deeper into the development of the site, the monument, and the museum and you will find a history of corruption, political ambition, and moral emptiness.

Today we have a president who lies and exploits the tragedy for his own tiny ego.

Today, we find ourselves living in a nation run by scoundrels who have lost all sense of what happened and what it means to be an american.  We have learned nothing from it except how to be small and hollow. 

Billions of dollars were spent to create a pit in memory to a world that never really existed.

Perhaps the real tragedy over these years has become not the terrible thing that happened on 911, but all the terrible things that have happened since.

That high level ornamentation is just so passé. That it's really for people who don't care. Or that it's a distraction in a world where no one cares. comments.name: Metrojournalist
comments.body:
Let's face it. Designer labels in fashion are aspirational for all but the uber-rich, just as new, big, and luxury homes or apartments are the aspiration for all homeowners. Ralph Lauren recognized this. Once he established himself, he had multiple tiers, making people of various income levels able to afford to wear his clothes, from those who shop at Walmart and Kohl’s to those who shop at Neiman-Marcus. I give him a lot of credit for his financial savvy as well as his designs which are as classic and timeless as they are aspirational as well as wearable.

Coach is another story. I started wearing Coach bags in the 1980s. They were made of high-quality leather, but they were heavy and ugly, but they conveyed the idea that I could afford better things. Then the company tried to appeal to younger customers with less disposable income. That didn’t last, so the company reinvented itself again, often with inspiration from higher end brands. And to make their merchandise even more aspirational, they raised their prices. Who would spend $500 on a Coach bag? Their apparel is usually meh, but what you showed here is unappealing. What’s with the gold dunce cap?

I still like Ralph Lauren’s old designs and think they’re beautiful. Coach, not so much. Also, I wish there were more Ralph Lauren home offerings.

comments.name: Mary

He brought  Southwest & yes, Preppy, with a twist. Fine fabrics, refined fit & some interesting detail and combinations. While premium in respects, & even moving into evening, it was & is America as his muse.  Did that change to the point of compounds in New Zealand because he dressed America's Olympians?  Too many designers now do seem to be chasing an ever morphing & fickle muse the world over.  If Lauren can be critiqued for not doing that, good for him, and good for Fashion.

comments.name: Lillas Pasta
comments.body: The BRICS proposition is a joke.  Most of the leaders of the countries involved are autocrats who have climbed to their positions in their national governments by various means, including repression, corruption, and manipulation.  They are fully aware that the "club" is populated by individuals of like backgrounds.  Trust is zero.  There are also serious inter-member disputes:  for example, China and India share a border that has witnessed numerous violent flare-ups and will no doubt continue to do so.  The idea of these nations operating in concert is laughable.  Fuggetaboutit.

comments.name: Ross

No pun was intended, I’m sure, when the author of this article said there are signs of cracks in the BRICS alliance.  

Modi’s statements on the war between Ukraine and Russia suggest there is at least a sliver of hope that BRICS can be a moderating influence and help bring the war to an end.   

By comparison, there are gaping fractures in the alliances formerly led by the Americans including NATO and there are no voices loud enough to overcome the bullhorn of the American president in his ego driven war against Iran.  

At the rate of America’s plummet to the depths no one will be surprised at the presence of observers from middle-power countries at a BRICS summit in the near future.

comments.name: SHT3
comments.body:
Welcome to reality, Messrs Xi, Modi ,Xi, de Lila etc. 
It is one thing to claim  BRICS - means an informal platform without written down rules, more like a club - und it is a completely more complicated to see rules and Goals and Mutual interests. Just look at the EU  - it is hard work to keep 27 states together. Now of course EU is a federation, while BRICS is informal a- so it is no counterweight to f i G7.
What made Russia drumming for this club, was mainly egoistic: 1) building a counterweight to the - in their eyes - "western dominated world order, 2) getting out of geopolitical isolation and3) changing the international finance market by reducing the influence of the US Dollar as reserve currency. Nothing of this happened so far. 
Now meanwhile China plays the most dominant and Industrial role, acting as its primary economic engine and the chief architect of its expansion to BRICS+. It views the bloc not merely as a 
trade group, but as a critical geopolitical tool of the global south, advance a multipolar world order and systematically  the "Western -centric Global Governance system". It counts for over 54% of the nominal GDP of the 5 original members combined. By integrating its Belt and Road Initiative, its Global Security Initiative and Global Development Initiative, it works on the realization of own goals and wishes the alliance to lobby for realigned voting quotes for the IMF and a soft de-dollarization.Modi is a geopolitical rival.
