Are people trying to get into the country or get out of the country?

I know of no one trying to get into a BRICS country. No one. China? Russia? India? Iran? South Africa?

I have met a ton of people who are happy to have gotten out of those places.

And guess where they're heading?

I had imagined Gloria going on and on, fighting good fights, and three decades from now laughing “this is what 120 looks like”.

comments.body: Thank you, Letty, just a million thanks. Just chiming in to say how many doors you and your Ms Magazine colleagues opened for our generation. I practiced law for 40 years, despite having doors slammed in my face in the early 1980’s because a few law firms openly told me they would not hire a woman. I’d been called “Little Lady “ in the courtroom, and I honestly didn’t think some of the older men knew how to react to me. But I had the strength and spirit of the women’s movement behind me, and I wasn’t going to go backwards. Thank you all from the bottom of my heart.

I just turned 25. Because of Gloria (and others like her), I've never known a world where I couldn't have my own bank account or pursue higher education. I work full-time and have the same rights as my male colleagues. I have my own apartment, my own vehicle, and my own credit. I am independent, and forever indebted to the women that came before me for the ability to be so. 

I've known so many men in my generation who lambast feminism as "woke", "ridiculous", and (perhaps most infuriating of all) "unnecessary". These men have mothers who work, female partners who split expenses with them 50/50, and women bosses who sign their paychecks - yet the necessity of equal rights is completely lost on them. We have a long way to go, but we've also come so far. Thank you, Gloria.

comments.name: Scaramouche
comments.body:
I was working for the city government that day and was attending a meeting in Queens with a state agency.  We were sitting in a conference room with a large picture window facing southwest toward the World Trade Center. 

Suddenly, someone said, “Look, the Works Trade Center is on fire!”  We all turned to look out the window and saw a hole in one of the towers and smoke a flame which was small at the time. 

 We continued to watch when suddenly I saw a large commercial airliner seemingly jump up from the bay and head up toward the second tower. I remember saying”Hey, that plane is getting too close!” thinking it was a mistake because of the smoke. 

Then I watched as it flew into the second tower and as a fireball broke out of the side of the building looking fake as if from a movie and my body tingled in shock.

We then realized it was an attack. But from the recesses of my mind I then remembered something g I must have read or heard before and I said out loud,
“Osama Bin Laden.”  And so began a day we will all never forget. 

As I jumped in my official vehicle to make my way back to my command, streets in front of police were blocked. The bridges were closed but I found a women police officer and identified my self and she said@I think the Triborough is still open.”  I then sped along grass highway medians and roadway u til I reached the bridge. I remember pausing before I hit the accelerator and thinking “I hope they don’t blow this up before I get across.”

An insightful article that everyone should read.  No magic bullet; just recognition the everyone has expectations of a better life with a new government.

I was in Aberdeen in June and found a rather desolate place of beautiful neighborhoods, lovely beaches and a nearly abandoned center-city. The people were welcoming and friendly but one had a strong sense of hopelessness after the North Sea oil boom years. 
As in most things, exploiting new oil fields is a conundrum: the environmental risks are not negligible but until a truly viable alternative to oil is found to power our economies and livelihoods - not just in Aberdeen but pretty much everywhere - allowing exploitable energy to sit idle seems a wasted opportunity. Exploitation is finite since the oil will run out and human beings will have to create new energy sources or radically adjust our daily lives to ones with much less of an environmental footprint. Norway doesn’t seem to have the navel-gazing, angst-ridden doubts that have characterized the UK governments’ indecisiveness on going forward. After the true disaster of Brexit going forward on exploiting a national resource of worldwide importance that would bring some wealth and energy stability back to Britain doesn’t seem like such a stretch.

I worked for 5 years in the UK oil patch and saw first hand the continent’s struggle to accept the difficult tradeoffs to create a sensible path to clean energy.  The UK and Europe won’t save the planet by burning fossil fuels from elsewhere while marching around wearing Greenpeace t-shirts.

comments.name: Victor
comments.body:
After WWII 12 million GI's returned to civilian life. Most were boys still living at home when the war began. But they returned as young men seeking to move out, marry and start a family.

We didn't rely neatly on the private sector to meet this crisis. And we recognized that profit margins would never be high enough to meet the needs of the working class.

Public housing was our answer. Vast numbers of substandard units were torn down and replaced by modern apartment buildings.

Mistakes were made. Chicago used public housing to impose neighborhood segregation and warehouse the poor. But New York expanded the concept by building subsidized apartments for both the working class and the middle class in the form of coops.

The underlying principle is simple. The market will never generate sufficient profit to meet our housing needs.

Just like the 50's and 60's, we need a bold extensive building program suitable for this generation.

While for now this is politically beyond our reach, the idea is not. And to achieve any bold idea we must push hard for its acceptance.

No great achievement has ever come from just being practical.

In my experience, Leimert Park has not been a welcoming neighborhood, when visiting friends in and around the area.  I sympathize with the interviewed residents who claim that it is, as I don't want to assume my experience is the norm, but controversies like these - undoubtedly escalated by social media - show that there is some level of underlying suspicion of anyone not Black shopping or exploring the neighborhood. 

At the same time, I have to wonder - what exactly has the city and local / community leadership been doing to support this neighborhood? The (city-owned) Vision Theatre has been closed for renovation since 2011 and missed many reopening deadlines. A jazz festival was supposed to take place in the area in July, and was mostly cancelled and scaled back. The article should have highlighted this context and recent events, as it's not clear to me what, if anything, community leaders are doing besides attacking or limiting any kind of "outside" interest in the area. 

LA is constantly changing, like all cities, and it's affecting all sorts of communities of color. Gentrification has pushed out Latinos from many Eastside neighborhoods into South LA, as the article references. As homeownership becomes ever more elusive and untenable for many, especially people of color, these communities are going to continue to disperse, fragment, and shift. 

It seems to me we should be attacking the rising cost of living and real estate instead of each other.

(It of course makes sense to talk about neighborhoods where most of the population is a certain race, due to segregation — but I don't think it's a problem if those demographics end up changing.)

However, this was a legitimate misunderstanding that blew up from I'm sorry, but purposeful stoking of the flames (really, you thought a RUNNING event using the terms "take back the streets" was actually offensive? Come on.). 

Public parks should be public spaces, and this was a wonderful opportunity for the older generations to show what real cultural acceptance looks like. It's a shame they opted for the scarcity mindset.

Thanks to Mr. Powell, 21, the voice of reason. It's a public park. You shouldn't need a permit fight, and the conditions to granting a permit even if you needed one being based on the race of the people participating is an outrage. 

Beyond this situation, left-wing activists need to understand that the focus on racial identity in situations like this (we are "protecting a black neighborhood", making sure "long term residents don't get pushed out") is *directly* responsible for the rise in the exact same type of rhetoric on the right! In the 90s, we'd reached the reasonable outcome that "we're all Americans and can live and work and do whatever we want". Apparently we are now back to 1960, where the longest term residents of your neighborhood can argue to keep others from living there based on their race, or even from owning a store based on the race (!), and this is ok because it is "punching up"? It's utter lunacy and just absolutely terrible for civic harmony.

In my youth the preeminent road race was the Mille Miglia, 992 miles from Brescia to Rome and back through old towns and villages pre-freeways, with no spectator barriers or sidewalks. 

Sir Stirling Moss showed it who was boss, winning non-stop apart from refuelling in his works Mercedes 300SLR at an average(!) speed of 99mph, wearing goggles before visors were invented, with small aero screens for protection.
His small navigator Denis Jenkinson deserved special praise, yelling directions over the deafening mechanical and road roar, looking down at his hand-drawn 'bog roll' as he unraveled it. His teammate finished second half an hour later. Several drivers and spectators were killed or injured.

Two years later I was opposite his pit at Aintree when he won the historic European Grand Prix in a British Vanwall Special.

comments.name: Rodrick Wallace
comments.body:
I am Deborah Wallace, a public health ecologist who in 2001 worked at a site represented by the NY News Guild (then called Newspaper Guild). I was on the executive committee and knew that Guild members were exposed to the pollutants issuing from Ground Zero.  Besides the reporters, three major employers had offices near WTC: Dow-Jones, Standard & Poors, and Reuters computer center. 

I worked with Guild leadership and with my husband's colleagues at the NYS Psychiatric Institute's Division of Epidemiology to find out what Guild members experienced and needed through focus groups. We found large differences in how the executives dealt with contamination of their buildings. Standard & Poors leaders really cared about their employees, had the building cleaned professionally more than once, and held meetings to hear about their concerns. The folks at the Reuters computer center had a much worse experience and worked in contamination. At least one ended up with WTC asthma.

Guild officers made sure that the affected members had opportunity for medical monitoring and treatment through the Guild's affiliation with the Communications Workers union. Many enrolled in the special health registry for long-term monitoring. 

I  received the Guild's Tom Keenan award for my service to these hidden heroes. A second edition of my book, In the Mouth of the Dragon: Toxic Fires in the Age of Plastics, has recently been published by Fire Engineering Books.
